screens.title: Other Storage Services & Data Migration Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build a practical mental model for three core AWS storage types that developers encounter frequently: block volumes, shared file systems, and managed relational databases. We’ll explain how Amazon Elastic Block Store provides low-latency block storage for a single EC2 host, how Elastic File System offers a mountable, shared file layer for many clients, and how RDS gives you managed relational engines when you need S Q L semantics and ACID properties. I will also walk you through migration options — network-based tools like DataSync, physical transfer devices like Snowball and Snowmobile, and database migration helpers — so you can match the right strategy to the dataset size and timing requirements. Finally, we’ll cover consistency models across these services and common developer mistakes, like assuming every storage service is strongly consistent. As you watch, think about a microservice you know and which storage type would be the simplest, most reliable fit. By the end you’ll be able to justify a storage choice for a real workload and pick a migration approach that balances speed, cost, and risk.

Other Storage Services & Data Migration

Understand EBS, EFS, and RDS, when each is appropriate for developer workloads, and how to move data to AWS safely at different scales.

EBS
Persistent block storage, single EC2 host, low latency.
EFS
Shared POSIX file system mountable by many clients.
RDS
Managed relational engines with ACID semantics.
In this lesson
Decide between block, file, and relational storage. Learn migration options and consistency patterns.
Coming up
  • When to use EBS, EFS, or RDS in a microservice architecture.
  • DataSync and Snowball migration patterns.
  • How consistency models affect reads and writes.
Visual Concept
EBS = single-host block disk
Think: an attached hard drive for one EC2 instance.
EFS = shared POSIX file system
Mount from many clients simultaneously.
RDS = managed relational engines
Use when you need SQL, joins, and ACID guarantees.
Explore Key Topics
Storage Comparison
Match latency and sharing needs.
Migration Tools
Network or physical transfer for scale.
Consistency Models
Design for eventual or strong reads.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives will guide your practical decisions as a developer working with storage on AWS. First, you will differentiate EBS, EFS, and RDS by access pattern and operational trade-offs so you can pick the right store for a given workload. For example, knowing that EBS is a single-instance block device helps you avoid using it for shared file storage needs. Second, you will identify when block or file storage is preferable to object storage or NoSQL, so you can match application requirements like low-latency random reads or POSIX semantics to the correct service. Third, you will understand the developer’s role when using RDS: how application code connects with S Q L drivers, and what operational tasks are managed for you. Lastly, you will explore migration tools and strategies so that you can plan migrations that balance time, cost, and risk. Each objective includes a competency milestone to verify that you can explain choices and propose a migration approach for a small project.

screens.title: Storage Comparison Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: Let's build a mental comparison matrix so you can choose storage deliberately. At one end, EBS provides block-level volumes attached to a single EC2 instance; it acts like a local disk, ideal for databases or applications needing raw block access and low latency. EFS offers a POSIX-compliant, mountable file system that multiple clients can access concurrently, which is useful for shared development environments or content management. RDS is a managed relational database service exposing S Q L and ACID guarantees, suitable for structured data and complex queries. S3 and DynamoDB remain reference points: S3 for immutable objects and large static assets, DynamoDB for fast key-value access and flexible schemas. A concrete example: an image pipeline might store originals and processed artifacts in S3, mount shared worker code on EFS for multiple processing nodes, and keep job metadata in DynamoDB. A common misconception is thinking file semantics are available on S3 — they are not; you cannot append to an S3 object the way you write to a file. Takeaway: always translate your application's access pattern — shared vs single host, object vs file, transactional S Q L vs key-value — into the correct storage category. Which service does your current project resemble?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Storage Matrix
Comparison

Storage Comparison Matrix

Use this checklist to map requirements to services.
EBS
  • Block storage for a single EC2 instance
  • Low-latency, raw disk access
  • Good for OS volumes and stateful DBs
EFS
  • POSIX file system mountable by many clients
  • Useful for shared code, config, or media libraries
  • Concurrent read/write across instances
RDS
  • Managed relational engines with ACID guarantees
  • Use standard SQL drivers; AWS handles patches and backups
  • Best for structured data and joins
Concrete Example
An image pipeline: S3 stores blobs, EFS stores shared processing code for many workers, DynamoDB holds job state, and EBS provides temporary scratch for a single high-performance instance.
Common Mistake
Assuming S3 behaves like a file system — you cannot append or open partial writes; you must overwrite objects.
Key Takeaway

Decide by access pattern: single-host block, multi-host POSIX file, or managed SQL for relational needs.

screens.title: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS)
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage for EC2. Think of EBS as an external hard drive attached to one server: your application running on that EC2 instance performs reads and writes to a device that behaves like a local disk. Developers interact with EBS by creating volumes, attaching them to instances, formatting the filesystem, and using standard file input and output; snapshots let you back up volumes. A concrete example is running a stateful database on EC2 where low-latency random input and output matters: you provision an EBS volume as the database data disk and tune IOPS accordingly. A common misconception is to try and share an EBS volume across multiple instances — EBS is tied to one instance per volume in typical usage. If you need shared access, mount EFS instead. Key operational notes: EBS is AZ-scoped for availability, snapshots are the recommended backup method, and you should plan for capacity and IOPS relative to your workload. Closing question: for a single-VM database that requires fast random reads, how would EBS shape your deployment and backup strategy?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › EBS Deep Dive
Definition

Amazon Elastic Block Store

Persistent block storage used as disks attached to a single EC2 instance. Format and use like a local drive.

How developers use EBS
  • Attach volumes to EC2 and format with a filesystem.
  • Use as primary storage for databases or OS volumes.
  • Back up using snapshots for point-in-time copies.
Concrete Example
An EC2-hosted PostgreSQL instance stores its data on an EBS volume that provides consistent low-latency reads and writes. Snapshots create backups for restore or cloning.
Common Mistake
Attempting to use a single EBS volume concurrently from multiple EC2 instances for shared storage — EBS is not a multi-writer shared filesystem.
When to pick EBS
Stateful workloads needing low-latency block access and a single host attachment.
# Conceptual steps (not executed here)
# 1. Create EBS volume
# 2. Attach to EC2 instance
# 3. Format and mount
sudo mkfs -t ext4 /dev/xvdf
sudo mkdir /data
sudo mount /dev/xvdf /data
Key Takeaway

EBS gives single-host block semantics — perfect for VM-local databases and OS volumes; use snapshots for backups.

screens.title: Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic File System is a managed, elastic file store that you mount over the network using NFS. Unlike EBS, EFS can be shared concurrently across multiple EC2 instances, containers, or supported Lambda functions, making it a natural choice where many processes need access to the same files, such as shared code repositories, content management, or configuration libraries. As a developer you mount the file system and access it with normal POSIX calls; applications see regular files and directories. A concrete scenario: several build servers mount the same EFS home directory so shared artifacts and caches remain consistent across workers. A frequent misconception is assuming EFS is as low-latency as local disks; network-backed file systems have higher latency and throughput characteristics that you should measure against your workload. EFS supports strong consistency for filesystem operations, so file updates are visible to other mounts reliably. Takeaway: choose EFS when you need multi-client access with POSIX semantics, and validate performance expectations during testing. Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) means mount efs for shared code, libraries, or content; it provides concurrent access and posix semantics but is network-backed.. In practical terms, elastic, shared posix file storage for many clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › EFS Deep Dive
Definition

Amazon Elastic File System

A managed, elastic, POSIX-compliant file system mountable by many clients over NFS.

Developer interactions
Mount via NFS and read/write files as usual. Useful for shared libraries, config, and content stores that require POSIX semantics.
Concrete Example
A CI cluster mounts EFS to share build caches and tools so each worker sees the same files without duplicating artifacts.
Common Mistake
Expecting local-disk latency. EFS is network-backed; test throughput and latency for your workload before committing to it.
When to pick EFS
Multi-client POSIX needs, shared configuration, or content libraries across instances and Lambda.
Mount Example
# Mount via NFS (conceptual)
sudo mount -t nfs4 -o nfsvers=4.1 fs-01234567.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs
Key Takeaway

EFS is your choice for multi-client, POSIX semantics. Validate performance expectations for network-backed file access.

screens.title: Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS)
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon RDS is a managed service that hosts relational database engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL, and it handles routine administrative tasks such as backups, patching, and failover. For a developer, RDS means you write S Q L with familiar drivers and let the service handle operational complexity. A concrete example is moving a legacy on-premises billing database to RDS: you retain the same schema and queries, but you no longer manage the underlying OS or software updates. RDS delivers strong consistency and ACID properties expected from relational databases, so transactional workloads and complex joins work as they do on-premises. A common misconception is that RDS eliminates the need to understand database design; it does not. You still model schemas, indexes, and queries for performance. Key developer responsibilities include managing connections, optimizing queries, and designing backups and read-replica strategies. Reflect: for an app needing strong transactional guarantees and complex joins, how would RDS simplify operations while keeping you focused on schema and queries? Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) means use rds when you need sql, acid guarantees, and reduced operational burden; you still own schema and query performance.. In practical terms, managed sql databases with acid guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › RDS Deep Dive
Definition

Amazon Relational Database Service

A managed relational database offering that supports engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL with ACID semantics.

Developer interactions
Connect with standard SQL drivers; RDS handles patching, backups, and failover tasks at the service layer.
Concrete Example
A legacy inventory system moves to RDS so developers keep the same queries while offloading backups and replication to the service.
Common Mistake
Assuming RDS removes the need to tune indexes and queries; performance remains a developer responsibility.
When to pick RDS
Transactional workloads, complex joins, and cases where ACID semantics matter.
Developer checklist
  • Use standard DB drivers to connect
  • Plan schema and indexes for queries
  • Design backup and read-replica strategies
Key Takeaway

RDS reduces operational work for relational databases while preserving expected SQL and transactional behavior; you still design for performance.

screens.title: Choosing Storage for Microservices
screens.narratorSegment: A practical way to decide is to map microservices to storage by looking at their access pattern and data shape. Consider a user profile service: it usually needs fast key-based access without complex joins, so a NoSQL store like DynamoDB often fits. An image processing service benefits from object storage like S3 for raw and processed images, because objects are large and immutable. A legacy user directory with complex relationships and transactional updates is a natural fit for RDS. For shared developer tooling or content libraries that many instances must read and write, EFS is appropriate. And where a single EC2-hosted application requires a performant disk for an on-disk database or state, EBS should be chosen. A common misconception is to default to S3 because it’s cheap — but S3 lacks POSIX semantics and is unsuitable when file-level operations or in-place file edits are required. Example: if multiple containers need to read and write a common configuration file, EFS solves the problem; using S3 would force workarounds. Takeaway: map each service to storage by asking three questions — who accesses the data, how is it accessed, and what consistency guarantees are required?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Microservice Mapping
Use Case Mapping

Choosing Storage for Microservices

Examples
  • User profile service → DynamoDB for fast key-value access
  • Image processing service → S3 for raw images and results
  • Legacy SQL app → RDS for ACID and joins
  • Shared code/config → EFS mounted across instances
  • Single-host DB or OS disk → EBS
Decision Tips
  1. Who needs access: single host or many?
  2. How is it accessed: file ops, object API, or SQL?
  3. Consistency: eventual or strong?
Analogy
Think: EBS is a personal laptop disk, EFS is a shared NAS, RDS is a managed office filing cabinet indexed for fast lookups, and S3 is a cloud locker for full objects.
Key Takeaway

Map services by access, API, and consistency to choose the storage that minimizes complexity and cost.

screens.title: Data Migration Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: When migrating data into AWS, the right strategy depends on dataset size, available network bandwidth, and how quickly you need the data available. For small datasets, direct uploads using the CLI or SDK are often simplest and low-cost. For larger or recurring transfers, DataSync automates and accelerates transfers between on-premises storage and AWS storage services such as S3, EFS, or FSx. For extremely large datasets where network transfer is impractical, physical devices like Snowball or Snowmobile let you ship data to AWS. For relational and NoSQL databases, Database Migration Service helps replicate and migrate data with minimal downtime. A concrete migration plan: for a 2 TB archive with limited bandwidth, choose Snowball; for nightly synchronization of a growing file share, use DataSync; for migrating a production RDBMS with near-zero downtime, consider DMS with continuous replication and a final cutover. A common misconception is treating one migration tool as universal — each tool is optimized for specific scenarios. Takeaway: evaluate size, time, and change rate before selecting a migration path. Data Migration Strategies means small sets → cli/sdk, recurring or networked → datasync, massive offline → snowball/snowmobile, database moves → dms.. In practical terms, pick a migration approach based on data size and network constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Migration Strategies
Process Flow

Data Migration Strategies

Select a migration approach by evaluating dataset size, change rate, and network capacity.

Small datasets
Use CLI or SDK uploads for files or objects; simplest for a few GBs to low TBs if network permits.
DataSync
Automates network transfers and syncs to S3, EFS, or FSx for recurring or one-time migrations.
Physical devices
Snowball or Snowmobile for very large datasets where shipping hardware is faster than network transfer.
Database migration
Use Database Migration Service to replicate and migrate relational or NoSQL databases with minimal downtime.
Concrete Planning Tip

screens.title: Data Consistency Models
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding consistency is vital when your application reads after writes or relies on synchronized state across services. Strong consistency means a read always reflects the most recent successful write — RDS, EBS, and EFS file operations typically provide strong consistency, which simplifies reasoning about state. Eventual consistency means that after a change, reads might temporarily return older values until updates propagate; this model is common in globally distributed object stores. S3 offers read-after-write consistency for new objects, meaning a read after creating a new object will succeed, but overwrite puts and deletes are eventually consistent and may return stale views briefly. DynamoDB offers both eventual and strong consistency modes: eventual by default for faster, cheaper reads, and an opt-in strong consistent read when you need the latest write. A concrete example: if you immediately read an object after overwriting it in S3, you may see the previous version briefly; implement retries or strong-read alternatives where required. A common misconception is assuming all AWS stores are strongly consistent by default. Takeaway: know the model for each service and design retry, versioning, or strongly-consistent-read strategies where needed.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Consistency Models
Definition

Data Consistency Models

Strong vs eventual vs read-after-write: choose patterns that preserve correctness for your application.

Strong consistency
Reads always reflect the most recent successful write. EBS, EFS, and RDS provide this for typical operations.
Eventual consistency
Reads may return stale data briefly while updates propagate. Implement retries, versioning, or strong reads if needed.
Read-after-write (S3)
S3 offers read-after-write for new objects, but overwrite PUTs and deletes are eventually consistent.
Concrete Example
After overwriting an object in S3, an immediate read might return the old version briefly. Plan retries or strong reads where you need the newest value.
Common Mistake
Assuming all services behave the same; verify each service’s model and design your application logic accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Design for the service’s consistency model: use retries, versioning, or strong reads when eventual consistency can impact correctness.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll build a practical mental model for three core AWS storage types that developers encounter frequently: block volumes, shared file systems, and managed relational databases. We’ll explain how Amazon Elastic Block Store provides low-latency block storage for a single EC2 host, how Elastic File System offers a mountable, shared file layer for many clients, and how RDS gives you managed relational engines when you need S Q L semantics and ACID properties. I will also walk you through migration options — network-based tools like DataSync, physical transfer devices like Snowball and Snowmobile, and database migration helpers — so you can match the right strategy to the dataset size and timing requirements. Finally, we’ll cover consistency models across these services and common developer mistakes, like assuming every storage service is strongly consistent. As you watch, think about a microservice you know and which storage type would be the simplest, most reliable fit. By the end you’ll be able to justify a storage choice for a real workload and pick a migration approach that balances speed, cost, and risk.

These learning objectives will guide your practical decisions as a developer working with storage on AWS. First, you will differentiate EBS, EFS, and RDS by access pattern and operational trade-offs so you can pick the right store for a given workload. For example, knowing that EBS is a single-instance block device helps you avoid using it for shared file storage needs. Second, you will identify when block or file storage is preferable to object storage or NoSQL, so you can match application requirements like low-latency random reads or POSIX semantics to the correct service. Third, you will understand the developer’s role when using RDS: how application code connects with S Q L drivers, and what operational tasks are managed for you. Lastly, you will explore migration tools and strategies so that you can plan migrations that balance time, cost, and risk. Each objective includes a competency milestone to verify that you can explain choices and propose a migration approach for a small project.

This screen re-centers the objectives on developer tasks. First, when differentiating storage services, you’ll practice describing why an image processing service uses object storage while a stateful database uses block storage. That habit prevents architecture mismatches. Second, when choosing block or file storage over object or NoSQL, you’ll consider concrete constraints: do you need POSIX file semantics or can you store immutable objects? Third, your role with RDS is to use standard S Q L drivers and rely on RDS for administrative tasks; this lets you focus on schema design and queries instead of backups and patching. Fourth, in planning migrations you’ll select DataSync for automated network transfers, Snowball for very large offline moves, or DMS for database migrations. Each objective is framed so you can demonstrate competency by explaining a case study and recommending a storage and migration plan.

Let's build a mental comparison matrix so you can choose storage deliberately. At one end, EBS provides block-level volumes attached to a single EC2 instance; it acts like a local disk, ideal for databases or applications needing raw block access and low latency. EFS offers a POSIX-compliant, mountable file system that multiple clients can access concurrently, which is useful for shared development environments or content management. RDS is a managed relational database service exposing S Q L and ACID guarantees, suitable for structured data and complex queries. S3 and DynamoDB remain reference points: S3 for immutable objects and large static assets, DynamoDB for fast key-value access and flexible schemas. A concrete example: an image pipeline might store originals and processed artifacts in S3, mount shared worker code on EFS for multiple processing nodes, and keep job metadata in DynamoDB. A common misconception is thinking file semantics are available on S3 — they are not; you cannot append to an S3 object the way you write to a file. Takeaway: always translate your application's access pattern — shared vs single host, object vs file, transactional S Q L vs key-value — into the correct storage category. Which service does your current project resemble?

Amazon Elastic Block Store provides persistent block-level storage for EC2. Think of EBS as an external hard drive attached to one server: your application running on that EC2 instance performs reads and writes to a device that behaves like a local disk. Developers interact with EBS by creating volumes, attaching them to instances, formatting the filesystem, and using standard file input and output; snapshots let you back up volumes. A concrete example is running a stateful database on EC2 where low-latency random input and output matters: you provision an EBS volume as the database data disk and tune IOPS accordingly. A common misconception is to try and share an EBS volume across multiple instances — EBS is tied to one instance per volume in typical usage. If you need shared access, mount EFS instead. Key operational notes: EBS is AZ-scoped for availability, snapshots are the recommended backup method, and you should plan for capacity and IOPS relative to your workload. Closing question: for a single-VM database that requires fast random reads, how would EBS shape your deployment and backup strategy?

Amazon Elastic File System is a managed, elastic file store that you mount over the network using NFS. Unlike EBS, EFS can be shared concurrently across multiple EC2 instances, containers, or supported Lambda functions, making it a natural choice where many processes need access to the same files, such as shared code repositories, content management, or configuration libraries. As a developer you mount the file system and access it with normal POSIX calls; applications see regular files and directories. A concrete scenario: several build servers mount the same EFS home directory so shared artifacts and caches remain consistent across workers. A frequent misconception is assuming EFS is as low-latency as local disks; network-backed file systems have higher latency and throughput characteristics that you should measure against your workload. EFS supports strong consistency for filesystem operations, so file updates are visible to other mounts reliably. Takeaway: choose EFS when you need multi-client access with POSIX semantics, and validate performance expectations during testing. Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) means mount efs for shared code, libraries, or content; it provides concurrent access and posix semantics but is network-backed.. In practical terms, elastic, shared posix file storage for many clients. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Amazon RDS is a managed service that hosts relational database engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL, and it handles routine administrative tasks such as backups, patching, and failover. For a developer, RDS means you write S Q L with familiar drivers and let the service handle operational complexity. A concrete example is moving a legacy on-premises billing database to RDS: you retain the same schema and queries, but you no longer manage the underlying OS or software updates. RDS delivers strong consistency and ACID properties expected from relational databases, so transactional workloads and complex joins work as they do on-premises. A common misconception is that RDS eliminates the need to understand database design; it does not. You still model schemas, indexes, and queries for performance. Key developer responsibilities include managing connections, optimizing queries, and designing backups and read-replica strategies. Reflect: for an app needing strong transactional guarantees and complex joins, how would RDS simplify operations while keeping you focused on schema and queries? Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS) means use rds when you need sql, acid guarantees, and reduced operational burden; you still own schema and query performance.. In practical terms, managed sql databases with acid guarantees. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A practical way to decide is to map microservices to storage by looking at their access pattern and data shape. Consider a user profile service: it usually needs fast key-based access without complex joins, so a NoSQL store like DynamoDB often fits. An image processing service benefits from object storage like S3 for raw and processed images, because objects are large and immutable. A legacy user directory with complex relationships and transactional updates is a natural fit for RDS. For shared developer tooling or content libraries that many instances must read and write, EFS is appropriate. And where a single EC2-hosted application requires a performant disk for an on-disk database or state, EBS should be chosen. A common misconception is to default to S3 because it’s cheap — but S3 lacks POSIX semantics and is unsuitable when file-level operations or in-place file edits are required. Example: if multiple containers need to read and write a common configuration file, EFS solves the problem; using S3 would force workarounds. Takeaway: map each service to storage by asking three questions — who accesses the data, how is it accessed, and what consistency guarantees are required?

When migrating data into AWS, the right strategy depends on dataset size, available network bandwidth, and how quickly you need the data available. For small datasets, direct uploads using the CLI or SDK are often simplest and low-cost. For larger or recurring transfers, DataSync automates and accelerates transfers between on-premises storage and AWS storage services such as S3, EFS, or FSx. For extremely large datasets where network transfer is impractical, physical devices like Snowball or Snowmobile let you ship data to AWS. For relational and NoSQL databases, Database Migration Service helps replicate and migrate data with minimal downtime. A concrete migration plan: for a 2 TB archive with limited bandwidth, choose Snowball; for nightly synchronization of a growing file share, use DataSync; for migrating a production RDBMS with near-zero downtime, consider DMS with continuous replication and a final cutover. A common misconception is treating one migration tool as universal — each tool is optimized for specific scenarios. Takeaway: evaluate size, time, and change rate before selecting a migration path. Understanding consistency is vital when your application reads after writes or relies on synchronized state across services. Strong consistency means a read always reflects the most recent successful write — RDS, EBS, and EFS file operations typically provide strong consistency, which simplifies reasoning about state. Eventual consistency means that after a change, reads might temporarily return older values until updates propagate; this model is common in globally distributed object stores. S3 offers read-after-write consistency for new objects, meaning a read after creating a new object will succeed, but overwrite puts and deletes are eventually consistent and may return stale views briefly. DynamoDB offers both eventual and strong consistency modes: eventual by default for faster, cheaper reads, and an opt-in strong consistent read when you need the latest write. A concrete example: if you immediately read an object after overwriting it in S3, you may see the previous version briefly; implement retries or strong-read alternatives where required. A common misconception is assuming all AWS stores are strongly consistent by default. Takeaway: know the model for each service and design retry, versioning, or strongly-consistent-read strategies where needed.
